note: Two instantiations per unit, one in baking and one in carpentry. copied_runs counts consecutive words, function words included, against the whole paper.

instantiations: To keep bread fresh longer, we built a storage plan for loaves, rolls, and a tin of dry crackers. Freshness checks and taste checks were both run on it.
To keep a table steady, we built a bracing plan for the legs, the apron, and the top. Load checks and wobble checks were both run on it.
First, warm the milk. Because a cold dough rises slowly, set the bowl near the stove. Then knead. On that basis, shape the loaf.
First, cut the board. Because a dull blade tears the grain, sharpen it. Then drill. On that basis, glue the joint.
Putting the dough in the oven, we found a rise of one third, a crumb with even holes, and a crust of even color, which shows the loaf baked well.
Putting the frame under load, we found a sag of one millimeter, joints that held, and legs that stayed square, which shows the frame was sound.
Second, we checked the bake. In the color test, every loaf came out deep gold, close to the color card.
Second, we checked the glue. In the strength test, every joint held firm, close to the rated load.
The baker can start the loaf early, leave it to rise, and catch the moment it springs. Meanwhile, the same bake survives a cool kitchen.
The carpenter can cut the tenon early, leave it to seat, and catch the moment it locks. Meanwhile, the same joint survives a damp shed.
Small changes to the recipe gave 12 trial loaves. Their rise was lower, and ours beat 10 of them, which shows the recipe gives both volume and an even crumb at once.
Small changes to the joint gave 12 trial frames. Their stiffness was lower, and ours beat 10 of them, which shows the joint gives both strength and a clean look at once.
We test how the loaf reacts to salt. Salt down by a pinch, the rise up by a finger. Also, the dough reacts more to less salt than to more. At the end, every trial still cleared the pan.
We test how the joint reacts to glue. Glue down by a drop, the hold up by a notch. Also, the joint reacts more to less glue than to more. At the end, every trial still held the shelf.
People always want a warm meal, and when supper is late, the cook must find the fastest dish.
People always want a level floor, and when the boards rock, the carpenter must find the worst spot.
For any stew, how to balance richness and cost is the hard part. Auguste Escoffier set down the mother sauces in 1903. That gives a cook a place to start.
For any shelf, how to balance strength and weight is the hard part. Thomas Chippendale set down his cabinet patterns in 1754. That gives a maker a place to start.
First, for this order, we need a recipe for a family of four, drawn from the pantry list, which can feed them for a week.
First, for this job, we need a cutting list for a bookcase, drawn from the timber in the rack, which can fill the wall.
Following the classic method, we must watch both flavor and texture, and the cost of butter should also be counted.
Following the shop standard, we must watch both strength and appearance, and the cost of hardwood should also be counted.
Second, so the family trusts the baking, we need to show in some way that this loaf keeps.
Second, so the client trusts the work, we need to show in some way that this joint holds.
Then, since oven heat is one thing that changes the crumb, we need a way to test it.
Then, since shop humidity is one thing that changes the glue, we need a way to test it.
Finally, we owe the client a note of under a page covering the recipe, the batch it produced, and how it tasted.
Finally, we owe the client a note of under a page covering the joint, the frame it produced, and how it held.
The layout of the bench is shown below.
The layout of the shop is shown below.
To make the bake repeatable, we set the following rules from the kitchen we have and from standard practice.
To make the build repeatable, we set the following rules from the timber we have and from shop practice.
We take it that the oven holds its heat. We take it that the cook, given two tins, picks the lighter one. We take it that the cook, given two tins, picks the taller one.
We take it that the bench stays flat. We take it that the maker, given two boards, picks the stiffer one. We take it that the maker, given two boards, picks the lighter one.
Here the names in the chart are the ones we build with. Any rare name is explained the first time it appears.
Here the names in the chart are the ones we cut with. Any rare name is explained the first time it appears.
To begin, we found 4 gaps in the bake log. The gaps fall on the days the oven was serviced. Given that, we treat them as days with no bake, and we copy the previous day's note.
To begin, we found 4 gaps in the cut list. The gaps fall on the days the saw was serviced. Given that, we treat them as days with no cutting, and we copy the previous day's note.
The two charts show that both doughs grew, and the rye grew more. One spans a hand's width, the other a thumb's width.
The two charts show that both boards moved, and the pine moved more. One spans a finger's width, the other a hair's width.
We can see the rye varies more than the wheat, and the two move together. This shows the rye is the lively one, and the two doughs rise as a pair.
We can see the pine varies more than the oak, and the two move together. This shows the pine is the lively one, and the two boards move as a pair.
A poolish is a preferment bakers use for long ferments. It keeps a memory of the last fold, and so it predicts the next rise. After comparing preferments, we chose it.
A sliding dovetail is a joint cabinetmakers use for long cases. It keeps a memory of the last cut, and so it predicts the next fit. After comparing joints, we chose it.
In this bake, the folds set how many times the dough is turned, the rest sets how long it sits, and the salt sets how tight it gets.
In this joint, the depth sets how far the cut goes, the width sets how wide it opens, and the angle sets how the faces meet.
First, we checked the dough. The charts show a steady climb and a slow fall in spring. At the same time, a poke test left a dent. So the dough is not ready and needs longer.
First, we checked the boards. The charts show a steady bow and a slow fall in stiffness. At the same time, a moisture test read high. So the boards are not ready and need drying.
Let the dough rest once. From the new charts it sits flat and springs back. The poke test now reads low. So the dough is ready. Since we rested it once, the rest count is one.
Let the boards dry once. From the new charts they sit flat and read even. The moisture now reads low. So the boards are ready. Since we dried them once, the drying count is one.
From the log, we score each rest time and keep the one with the best score. After that, we bake and record the rise.
From the log, we score each glue and keep the one with the best score. After that, we clamp and record the hold.
To judge the bake, a crumb check is needed. If the holes are even and random, the crumb behaves like a good loaf. We use a simple score.
To judge the joint, a fit check is needed. If the gaps are small and random, the joint behaves like a good fit. We use a simple score.
The chart shows the scores all clear the line we set. That is what lets us bake every day.
The chart shows the scores all clear the line we set. That is what lets us glue every joint.
The baked color tracks the target. It is closest while the oven is steady. At the turning point the loaf still colors, but a pale patch remains.
The cut tracks the line. It is closest while the saw is steady. At the turning point the cut still follows, but a rough patch remains.
Since each bake costs charcoal, baking too often wastes fuel, and we think the cook should pick the day with care. Days split into busy and quiet. Bake only on a busy day.
Since each cut costs a blade, cutting too often wastes edges, and we think the maker should pick the piece with care. Pieces split into straight and twisted. Cut only a straight piece.
The rolling-pin test reads the dough. Take the last few folds as the example. When the short folds sit above the long ones, the dough is rising; the other way, it is collapsing.
The straightedge test reads the board. Take the last few cuts as the example. When the short cuts sit above the long ones, the board is crowning; the other way, it is cupping.
If every fold lines up, the dough will spring. But a perfect line of folds is uncommon, so we treat eight rising folds as enough.
If every edge lines up, the board will sit flat. But a perfect line of edges is uncommon, so we treat eight true edges as enough.
The two charts disagree, so the two doughs want different handling. The quiet stretches mean leave them alone. From this we mark each dough ready or not.
The two charts disagree, so the two boards want different handling. The quiet stretches mean leave them alone. From this we mark each board ready or not.
A plain average is a poor guide, since it says nothing about the worst loaf. We use the worst slice instead, which starts from that average.
A plain average is a poor guide, since it says nothing about the worst joint. We use the worst cut instead, which starts from that average.
The old score estimates the worst loaf in a batch. It ignores how faults add up, and it misses the tail. Two bakers proposed a better score to fix both.
The old score estimates the worst joint in a run. It ignores how faults add up, and it misses the tail. Two makers proposed a better score to fix both.
To get a loaf that is both tall and even, we search many shapes and keep the plausible ones. In the end, a cap on the worst slice picks the loaf. Going tin by tin, we finish the batch.
To get a frame that is both stiff and light, we search many layouts and keep the plausible ones. In the end, a cap on the worst joint picks the frame. Going piece by piece, we finish the job.
Because the cook dislikes waste, every choice chases flavor and is held back by cost. So we set two goals.
Because the maker dislikes waste, every choice chases strength and is held back by weight. So we set two goals.
This search keeps the good candidates and spreads them out. Because it serves both goals, we use it. The steps follow.
This search keeps the good candidates and spreads them out. Because it serves both goals, we use it. The steps follow.
Step one, mix a batch and rank it. Here, one loaf beats another when it is no worse on every count and better on one. Step two, vary the batch. Step three, keep the best. Step four, stop.
Step one, cut a set and rank it. Here, one joint beats another when it is no worse on every count and better on one. Step two, vary the set. Step three, keep the best. Step four, stop.
We first get a set of plausible loaves. As the rise grows, the worst slice gets worse. To settle on one loaf, we cap that slice.
We first get a set of plausible frames. As the stiffness grows, the worst joint gets worse. To settle on one frame, we cap that joint.
Bakers care about a fallen loaf and shrug off a tall one, and an older writer proposed measuring only the falls. We agree. So we measure only the falls.
Makers care about a split joint and shrug off a tight one, and an older writer proposed measuring only the splits. We agree. So we measure only the splits.
The chart shows the bake. We see it loads the rye when the rye is cheap, shifts to wheat when the rye misbehaves, and holds flour back when both misbehave.
The chart shows the build. We see it loads the pine when the pine is cheap, shifts to oak when the pine misbehaves, and holds timber back when both misbehave.
For instance, in the busy week the rye dominated. The batch ends at a full rack, the average week feeds the shop, and the best week is the second.
For instance, in the busy week the pine dominated. The job ends at a full order, the average week fills the shop, and the best week is the second.
To show the recipe is the one to keep, we check it from the crumb side and from the keeping side.
To show the joint is the one to keep, we check it from the fit side and from the load side.
For the crumb, we use a handful of everyday measures. The numbers, worked out by hand, sit in the chart below.
For the fit, we use a handful of everyday measures. The numbers, worked out by hand, sit in the chart below.

The numbers come in under the line we care about, near the bottom of the scale, so the bake is very close. The other score sits near the top, so the recipe explains the rise. This lets us plan the next bake.

The numbers come in under the line we care about, near the bottom of the scale, so the fit is very close. The other score sits near the top, so the joint explains the strength. This lets us plan the next piece.
First, take the week before the holiday. The rye sprang by a large margin. Following the plan, we started the wheat early and let it ride. Over that week the batch gained plenty.
First, take the week before the deadline. The pine ran true by a large margin. Following the plan, we started the oak early and let it ride. Over that week the job gained plenty.

From midweek to the weekend, the rye collapsed and slumped. We caught it and switched to wheat. The loss over those days stayed small. After the test, the bake gets through a bad week and wastes little.
From midweek to the weekend, the pine twisted and cupped. We caught it and switched to oak. The loss over those days stayed small. After the test, the build gets through a bad week and wastes little.
The shake test starts from our bake and nudges each tin's dough by a small share, making several new bakes. The nudged dough stays within a tenth, and the water is reset to match.
The shake test starts from our build and nudges each piece's cut by a small share, making several new builds. The nudged cut stays within a tenth, and the glue is reset to match.
From the chart, the nudged bakes fell short by a clear margin. Only a few beat ours. The result points to steady tracking, calm handling, and a good yield.
From the chart, the nudged builds fell short by a clear margin. Only a few beat ours. The result points to steady tracking, calm handling, and a good yield.
Given the swings in flour supply over the period, the price jumps and the new shop rules, we go on to test the recipe.
Given the swings in timber supply over the period, the price jumps and the new shop rules, we go on to test the joint.
One year brought a new mill. The next brought a dry spell. So shifts in supply, weather, and local rules all change the bake. The shop then changes its order to cope.
One year brought a new yard. The next brought a wet spell. So shifts in supply, weather, and local rules all change the build. The shop then changes its order to cope.
By nudging the amount up and down, we set the salt at three levels and the yeast at three levels.
By nudging the amount up and down, we set the glue at three levels and the clamp time at three levels.

Plainly, less salt gives a better loaf, and the dough reacts more to salt than to yeast. In detail, salt down a step with yeast fixed lifts the loaf. Yeast down a step with salt fixed lifts it less. Also, adding hurts less than taking away.

Plainly, less glue gives a tighter joint, and the joint reacts more to glue than to clamp time. In detail, glue down a step with the clamp fixed lifts the hold. Clamp time down a step with glue fixed lifts it less. Also, adding hurts less than taking away.
After the amounts change, we reuse the shake test above, so the recipe still holds. In detail, we shake each version many times.
After the amounts change, we reuse the shake test above, so the joint still holds. In detail, we shake each version many times.
The recipe draws on baking and on bookkeeping, and it rests on the classic crumb method and the newer scoring method. Also, the timing rule comes from long use and has earned trust.
The joint draws on layout and on bookkeeping, and it rests on the classic fit method and the newer scoring method. Also, the timing rule comes from long use and has earned trust.
Because the scoring method has its limits, the recipe assumes the crumb spreads evenly. Other shapes need a different approach. With only one week's loaves, how far the recipe travels is still open.
Because the scoring method has its limits, the joint assumes the load spreads evenly. Other shapes need a different approach. With only one week's pieces, how far the joint travels is still open.
To the client. From the bake team. About the bread. Dated the Monday after delivery. This note covers the recipe, how it holds up, how it reacts, and what it yields.
To the client. From the shop team. About the frame. Dated the Monday after delivery. This note covers the joint, how it holds up, how it reacts, and what it yields.

Everyone knows a loaf depends on reading the dough. We use a simple preferment to guess the next rise. Because too many bakes waste fuel, we check the dough first. In the end, we set a target and cap the worst loaf.

Everyone knows a frame depends on reading the timber. We use a simple gauge to guess the next fit. Because too many cuts waste blades, we check the board first. In the end, we set a target and cap the worst joint.
At the same time, the cap can be moved to suit how bold the client feels, so the bake fits anyone.
At the same time, the cap can be moved to suit how bold the client feels, so the build fits anyone.
The batch grew past triple, the typical week feeds the shop, and the best week was the busiest, so the recipe earns its keep. The quietest week still broke even, so the bake can change course fast.
The order grew past triple, the typical week fills the shop, and the best week was the busiest, so the joint earns its keep. The quietest week still broke even, so the build can change course fast.

Over the early years the shop was calm. We favored the rye and kept wheat aside. The later years turned choppy. One year we bought rye low. The next we switched to wheat before the slump. The whole stretch ended well ahead.

Over the early years the shop was calm. We favored the pine and kept oak aside. The later years turned choppy. One year we bought pine low. The next we switched to oak before the slump. The whole stretch ended well ahead.
So the recipe can match the baking to the flour on hand, and stop early when a loaf turns. If you want more detail, we would be glad to walk through it.
So the joint can match the cutting to the timber on hand, and stop early when a piece turns. If you want more detail, we would be glad to walk through it.
